title: Carly Simon Reveals Parkinson’s Disease Diagnosis: ‘I Have Not Stopped Living and I Have Not Stopped Working’
full_text: Jul 27, 2026 5:15am PT Carly Simon Reveals Parkinson’s Disease Diagnosis: ‘I Have Not Stopped Living and I Have Not Stopped Working’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Carly Simon Reveals Parkinson’s Disease Diagnosis: ‘I Have Not Stopped Living and I Have Not Stopped Working’ 13 minutes ago Bill Oddie, Wildlife Presenter and Comedian, Dies at 85 3 hours ago Dylan Mulvaney Fires Back After Trump Mocks Her and Kaitlan Collins in White House Correspondents’ Dinner Speech: ‘Actually the Greatest Compliment of All’ 3 hours ago See All Getty Images for NARAS Carly Simon has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. The 83-year-old singer-songwriter, best known for her 1972 hit “You’re So Vain,” revealed the news on Monday in a statement (via People ). “So many people have written to me, kindly wondering about my relative silence, asking how I am and what I have been doing. The truth is, I’ve been learning how to live with Parkinson’s disease,” Simon said. Related Stories Deep Com Roots Sells ‘Summer Days’ to Half the World, as ISII Group Rolls on ‘Amor de Dios’ With Belen Rueda (EXCLUSIVE) “It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it, and to decide how much I wanted to say about it publicly,” she continued. “Parkinson’s is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable. Some days I’m so tired I can’t get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work, and feel like myself.” Popular on Variety Parkinson’s disease, a neurological disorder that effects nerve cells in the brain, does not currently have a cure. Symptoms include tremors, stiffness, difficulty balancing and slowness of movement. Simon said that she was diagnosed after her mobility continued to worsen following replacement surgeries on her knees and one hip. “Eventually, there were periods when I could not walk without considerable help,” the Grammy winner wrote. “My family and I knew that something more was going on. After an extensive evaluation at the Mayo Clinic, I was diagnosed with Parkinson’s.” Though Simon has been affected physically, she has also struggled with “anxiety, depression, exhaustion and apathy” after her diagnosis. “That has been one of the hardest things to explain,” she said. “It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list.” In addition to Parkinson’s, Simon also revealed that she was previously diagnosed with basal cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer, and underwent surgery for it amid her Parkinson’s treatment. “The cancer was removed, but the surgery affected my appearance and made me more self-conscious about being seen in public,” Simon said. “I have always been more critical of my appearance than anyone else could possibly imagine (check out the irony of having written ‘You’re So Vain’), and this gave my inner critic quite a lot of new material.” Simon has stayed out of the spotlight in recent years, with her last public performance being in March 2018. But despite her health struggles, she assured fans that she has “not stopped living” and “not stopped working.” In fact, she has written a new album, titled “Comes in Waves,” her first full-length effort since 2008. “Working on the music gave shape to days that did not always have much shape. It gave me somewhere to go without having to leave the room. It reminded me that illness can change your life without becoming the whole of your life,” she wrote. “I do not consider Parkinson’s a gift or a blessing. It is neither. It is difficult, frustrating, and sometimes frightening. I am still learning how to live with it and how to accept it without feeling that I have surrendered something essential.” Simon concluded her statement by saying: “These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different. title: Thabo Rametsi Unveiled As Apartheid Era Music Legend Hugh Masekela In First Look Image For Bill Condon’s ‘The Road Home’
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Thabo Rametsi Unveiled As Apartheid Era Music Legend Hugh Masekela In First Look Image For Bill Condon’s ‘The Road Home’ Oscar Documentary Contender ‘House Of Hope’ Secures North American Distribution Film Financiers & Producers Flock To Inaugural African Film Investor Roundtable In Cape Town View All July 27, 2026 5:01am The Road Home South African actor, writer, director and producer Thabo Rametsi ( Silverton Siege ) has been unveiled with in his role as activist and music legend Hugh Masekela in Bill Condon’s The Road Home as the filming continues in South Africa . A first look image released by the film’s backers and producers Canal+, Studiocanal and Flora Film as well as South African co-producer Blue Ice, shows Rametsi as Masekela, who lived in exile in the UK and the U.S. for 30 years after fleeing his native South Africa in the wake of the 1960 Sharpeville Massacre, playing his trumpet. The film follows Masekela as he finds himself at a crossroads when the Anti-Apartheid Movement, led by anti-apartheid advocate and mentor Archbishop Trevor Huddleston, launches a boycott against his friend Paul Simon over his township music-inspired album ‘Graceland’, accusing Simon of violating the United Nations’ Cultural Boycott. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Film Financiers & Producers Flock To Inaugural African Film Investor Roundtable In Cape Town News 'Terminator 2: Judgment Day' Sets 35th Anniversary Global Re-Release Masekela, who saw music as a powerful weapon in the anti-apartheid struggle, would split with Huddleston to join forces with fellow exile and lifelong collaborator, powerhouse vocalist Miriam ‘Mama Africa’ Makeba to create the Graceland band, a super group designed to bring South Africa’s voice to the world. As previously announced, Rametsi is joined in the cast by Guy Pearce as Huddleston; Johnny Flynn as Simon and Cynthia Erivo as Makeba. “When you tell the story of Giants you must shout it from the highest mountain. These are our giants and this film is the highest mountain we could find. We hope our humble tribute honours them accordingly,” said Rametsi, who is EP on the film. Condon ( Gods and Monsters ) directs from an original script written by Michael Bronner ( The Mauritanian, United 93 ), from a story by Bronner and Zakes Mda. The Canal+ and Studiocanal-backed feature is produced by Academy Award-Nominated producer Laura Bickford ( Traffic, Che Part 1 and Part 2, Arbitrage ), Bronner, Greg Yolen ( Kiss of the Spider Woman, The Good Liar ), and Anant Singh ( Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom, Sarafina! ), in association with Blue Ice’s producers Tebogo Maila and Adam Friedlander and with executive producers Fiona Druckenmiller, and Rametsi. title: Diego Luna To Receive Honorary Heart Of Sarajevo Award
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Sarajevo Film Festival Unveils Full Competition Lineup European Film Academy Chief Matthijs Wouter Knol & Greek Filmmaker Athina Rachel Tsangari Join Emily Watson On Sarajevo Film Festival Jury Asghar Farhadi To Receive Honorary Award At Sarajevo Film Festival View All July 27, 2026 4:57am Diego Luna Photo courtesy of Corey Nickols Diego Luna is set to be awarded an Honorary Heart of Sarajevo Award at the upcoming Sarajevo Film Festival in recognition of his career and contribution to world cinema. The Mexican actor-director-producer, whose work spans across film, TV and theater, will touch down at the Bosnian festival to present his latest directorial feature Ashes , which premiered at Cannes earlier this year. Luna will also give a masterclass, sharing his experience and perspectives on contemporary artistic practice with emerging talents, film professionals and festival audiences. Related Stories Festivals Sarajevo Film Festival Unveils Full Competition Lineup Festivals European Film Academy Chief Matthijs Wouter Knol & Greek Filmmaker Athina Rachel Tsangari Join Emily Watson On Sarajevo Film Festival Jury Luna’s international breakout performance was in Alfonso Cuarón’s 2001 title Y tu mama también , a role that established him as one of Mexico’s top screen talents. He went on to collaborate with directors such as Steven Spielberg, David Trueba, Gus Van Sant, Harmony Korine and Agustín Diaz Yanes. Watch on Deadline More recently, he starred in and executive produced the Disney+ series Andor , which saw him earn two Golden Globe nominations and two Critics’ Choice Award nominations for his work in both seasons. The series earned eight Emmy nominations for its first season and 14 for its second season, including Outstanding Drama Series. Luna also received two Normal Felton Award nominations alongside his team in the PGA Awards for his work as a producer in Andor . He recently starred in Netflix’s México 86 on which he also serves as executive producer and will appear in the thriller Eleven Days and Disney’s live-action adaptation of Tangled . Luna’s further credits include: Bill Condon’s Kiss of the Spider Woman ; La Máquina , which he also produced and starred in alongside Gael García Bernal; Netflix’s Narcos: México ; Star Wars: Rogue One ; and Bread & Circus . As a director, Luna made his debut with the documentary J.C. Chávez in 2007. His first narrative feature, Abel , earned the Horizontes Latinos Award at the San Sebastián International Film Festival and a Mexican Academy Award for Best Screenplay, which he co-wrote. He later director Mr. Pig , which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival. Beyond his creative work, Luna is deeply committed to social impact initiatives. In 2005, he co-founded Ambulante, a traveling documentary film festival created to foster cultural exchange. The festival was founded alongside García Bernal, Pablo Cruz, Elena Fortesand El Día Después, a Mexico City-based NGO that connects citizens with longstanding organizations to drive civic engagement and social change. “A quarter of a century ago, Diego Luna won our hearts with his unforgettable performance in Y Tu Mamá También ,” said Jovan Marjanović, Director of the Sarajevo Film Festival. “We hoped then and know now that we were witnessing the emergence of an artist who would never case to explore and surprise, moving seamlessly from major Hollywood productions to intimate human stories that reveal the richness of Latin American culture. Through his exceptional body of work, Diego Luna has left a profound mark on contemporary cinema, and it is our great honor to present him with the Honorary Heart of Sarajevo.” Luna added: “It’s been many years since I’ve wanted to go to Sarajevo. So many colleagues have spoken beautifully about the festival and their personal experience there. I feel honored with the recognition of my work and very excited to share Ashes with the audience.” The 32 nd Sarajevo Film Festival will take place from August 14-21, 2026. title: Deep Com Roots Sells ‘Summer Days’ to Half the World, as ISII Group Rolls on ‘Amor de Dios’ With Belen Rueda (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Jul 27, 2026 4:43am PT Deep Com Roots Sells ‘Summer Days’ to Half the World, as ISII Group Rolls on ‘Amor de Dios’ With Belen Rueda (EXCLUSIVE) The news comes just after fully English-language ‘La Cathédrale,’ with Will Keen (‘The Crown’) and ’One Piece' star Taz Skylar, also goes into production By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Buzz Title ‘Third Wheel,’ an ‘Allegory of Post-Colonial Africa,’ Brought to Market at Fantasia’s Frontières (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago ‘Sherlock’ Creator Steven Moffat Set as International Guest of Serielizados – Barcelona Series Festival (EXCLUSIVE) 6 days ago World Cup Final Ratings Skyrocket Across Europe, Despite England and France Losses 7 days ago See All Belén Rueda in 'Amor de Dios' Credit: Daniel Mayrit Flexing its muscles as one of the biggest new kids on its film industry block, Spain’s ISII Group has gone into production on “Amor de Dios” headlined by “The Orphanage” star Belén Rueda and produced by ISII banner label Inefable Productions. The news comes as ISII Group distribution-sales house Deep Com Roots has sold “Summer Days” to half the world’s major markets and cameras have rolled on “La Cathédrale,” Inefable’s first fully English production starring “One Piece” icon Taz Skylar . Related Stories Deep Com Roots Sells ‘Summer Days’ to Half the World, as ISII Group Rolls on ‘Amor de Dios’ With Belen Rueda (EXCLUSIVE) As a mark of its step-up in scale, ISII Group now has four films in production in 2026 and another quartet released or awaiting release, including Spanish Western “Trinidad,” an ambitious Wild West-set Spanish family saga led by “Your Fault’s” Gabriela Andrada, Paz Vega and Karla Sofía Gascón. All ISII Group titles are sold and distributed in Spain by Deep Com Roots, a strategic partner. Popular on Variety ‘Summer Days’ Closes Half the World “Summer Days” weighs in as a sun-drenched erotic drama with a thriller edge. Headed by Maggie Civantos , star of “Locked Up,” “Money Heist” creator Alex Pina’s first international breakout, “Summer Days” has closed Latin America, bought by Brazil’s Sofa Digital , plus Germany, Austria and Switzerland (Busch Media Group) and CIS (Kinologistika). Tokyo’s Aya Pro has licensed Japan, Mumbai’s PictureWorks India, distributor of Anatomy of a Fall and Flow, has acquired rights to India, and Scene & Sound those to South Korea. “Summer Days” (“Días de agosto”) begins with college students Juan (Pau Simón, “Nudes”) and Gabriela (Berta Galo, “La moderna”) escaping to his family beachside chalet for an idyllic summer. The film is described as a romantic drama. It acquires almost immediately, however, an erotic charge, in dialog and the arrival of Juan’s father Fernando (Roberto Álamo, “Riot Police”) with his much younger girlfriend Monica (Civantos). Juan and Monica’s feelings for each other build, mixing Juan’s resentment for his father leaving his mother and impossible-to-ignore physical attraction. “Deep Com Roots attended Cannes Market for the first time and was met with strong interest from the international market. Among our slate, Summer Days was one of the films that attracted the most attention from the buyers,” Emir Duzel, Deep Com Roots head of international sales, told Variety. “We believe its powerful story and the strong sense of tension made the film especially appealing. We are currently continuing negotiations for distribution deals for several more territories.” Early fruit of the ISII Group’s new talent support, “Summer Days” is based on a screenplay by David Sueiro, which was one of the seven fiction winners in the ISII Group’s first Break on Time ’59 national screenplay competition in 2024. It also marks a return to fiction of versatile director Chema del Prado, behind “IsiDisi,” a Spanish gross-out classic. Maggie Civantos in ‘Summer Days’ ‘Amor de Dios,’ Led Belén Rueda, Goes Into Production Also the female lead in Alejandro Amenábar’s Academy Award winner “The Sea Inside” and star of upscale genre hits “Julia’s Eyes” and “The Body,” in “Amor de Dios,” Rueda plays Sara Lanes, a renowned dancer and choreographer now living in Paris. When flamenco school Amor de Dios, once rated the world’s best, announces its closure, Sara returns to Madrid with disciple Ángela hoping to save the place where her own career began. “At the School, Sara reencounters a past she has never been able to leave behind. That and her own physical decline turns her return into a profoundly personal journey where she has to decide what she is willing to sacrifice in order to preserve her legacy,” says the synopsis. Inspired in its origins by an original idea by Spanish cinema great Carlos Saura, “Amor de Dios” is also produced by Inefable Productions Key cast also takes in Asier Etxeandia, co-star of Pedro Almodóvar’s “Pain and Glory,” and celebrated French dancer Soleila Chaou, Spanish National Ballet principal dancer Irene Tena and Tania Santana (“Love on a Tightrope”). Scheduled for release in 2027, “Amor de Dios” marks the awaited fiction feature debut of Paula Palacios, winner of the IDA Netflix 2022 Global Emerging Filmmaker Award and a double Goya best doc feature nominee for two stirring and affecting films, set against the context of African immigration to Europe: “Drowning Letters” (“Cartas Mojadas,” 2020) and “My Brother Ali,” (2024). “La Cathédrale,” Headlined by Will Keen and Taz Skylar “A new push for ISII Group’s fiction division,” it has noted, “La Cathédrale,” a double redemption thriller, turns on Thomas (Keen), a renowned violinist, who struggles to rebuild his life after the murder of his teenage daughter. When he agrees to take part in a restorative justice process with the man convicted of her killing (Skylar), the discovery of a mysterious violin among her belongings sets him on what the synopsis calls “a relentless search for the truth.” Beyond Slylar, “La Cathédrale” stars Keen, the distinguished British theatre actor and Private Secretary Michael Adeane in “The Crown,” Venice Horizons best actress Award winner Marta Nieto (“Mother”), Ronald Guttman, whose prolific and long career takes in “The Hunt for Red October,” “Lost” and “Mad Men”; and Catalan actor-pianist Peter Vives (“The Time in Between”). The film stands out for its “narrative tension, a powerful soundtrack and an immersive atmosphere,” Deep Com Roots has said. Now shooting in the Canary Islands, in Tenerife and Las Palmas, ““La Cathédrale” reflects director Eduardo Cubillo’s fascination with restorative justice. “Two people who seem irreconcilable – filled with hatred and countless grievances – can, through a simple conversation – which may or may not be difficult – end up feeling liberated in a way that has to be seen to be believed; it’s truly magical,” he has said. The film is written by Cubillo and scribe-helmer José Ortuño (“The Extraordinary Tale”). Taz Skylar in ‘La Cathédrale’ Deep Com Roots’ Slate “At ISII Group, we conceive each project not only from its creative ambition, but also the commercial career it can have inside and outside Spain,” said ISII Group President Silvia Carvalho. “So we have developed a structure which integrates development, financing, production, services, distribution and sales, with Deep Com Roots as the sales agent on all of our catalog,” she added. “‘Summer Days’ pre-sales and the interest generated by ‘La Cathédrale,’ ‘Amor de Dios’ and ‘Trinidad’ confirm that this model allows us to create value and market opportunities from the first stages of every film.” “Trinidad,” directed by Laura Alvea and José Ortuño, bows Nov. 2026. Gleaning great reviews, beginning in 1969 when Spain was still under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, “Tal vez” charts the perhaps requited love of Canary Islands poet Natalia Sosa Ayala (“Hierro”) for trapeze artist Pinito del Oro (Adriana Ugarte, “Juileta”), star of New York’s Ringling Brothers. Bowed July 10, it is directed by Arima León, turning on their encounter and their correspondence afterwards. Winner of the 2025 Break on Time competition, “Desde Arriba,” a father-son relationship dramedy, is now in post-production. Martín Cuervo directs from a screenplay by Arturo Ruiz Serrano and José Manuel Carrasco. A realist survival thriller starring Milena Smit (“Parallel Mothers”) and Irene Escolar (“Tell Me Who I Am”) “My Zone” shot in the Canary Islands of Gran Canaria and Fuerteventura from May. It marks the feature debut of best short fiction Goya winner Cristián Beteta (“Ángulo muerto”). Directed by Violeta Salama (“Alegría”), “Auri,” starring Cristina Marcos (“Maravillas,” “Locked Up”), a comedy turning on a housewife’s later life revolution, bowed in April in Spain. ‘Trinidad’ (L-R) Gabriela Andrada, Paz Vega and Karla Sofía Gascón Gabriela Andrada, Paz Vega and Karla Sofía Gascón in ‘Trinidad’. title: Locarno’s StepIn Focuses on ‘Power, People, Data and the Future of Film’: ‘The Counter-Algorithm Is a Human Being Who Gives a Damn’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Jul 27, 2026 4:18am PT Locarno’s StepIn Focuses on ‘Power, People, Data and the Future of Film’: ‘The Counter-Algorithm Is a Human Being Who Gives a Damn’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Locarno’s StepIn Focuses on ‘Power, People, Data and the Future of Film’: ‘The Counter-Algorithm Is a Human Being Who Gives a Damn’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Locarno’s First Look Section Reveals Six Uruguayan Titles, From Family Stories to Drama About Desire That ‘Persists Across Oceans’ 1 week ago Rosemary Who? Get Ready for Emma’s Baby as ‘Birth’ Seduces Tallifornia Film Fund With ‘Grotesque and Terrifying’ Take on Pregnancy (EXCLUSIVE) 2 weeks ago See All StepIn speakers Courtesy of Locarno Pro Now in its 15th year, Locarno’s think tank StepIn will debate “Power, People, Data and the Future of Film.” “Last year, StepIn focused on one of the defining qualities of independent cinema: the willingness to embrace risk. One of the strongest conclusions from those discussions was that playing it safe is rarely the smartest strategy,” said Marcello Paolillo, Locarno Pro , StepIn and U30 Project Manager. Related Stories Deep Com Roots Sells ‘Summer Days’ to Half the World, as ISII Group Rolls on ‘Amor de Dios’ With Belen Rueda (EXCLUSIVE) “After all, audiences fall in love with films because they’re original, surprising and emotionally truthful. Yet we are increasingly surrounded by algorithms, sophisticated data analysis, AI and systems designed to reduce uncertainty, predict outcomes and optimize decisions.” Popular on Variety The event will explore how power structures, human capital, politics, AI, data-driven decision-making and increasing industry consolidation are reshaping the future of independent cinema. Approaching the subject from “four interconnected perspectives,” it will allow the participants to discuss the following topics: “Films vs. Formula: Algorithms, Consolidation and Creative Freedom,” “Sustainable Indie Financing: Connecting Private Investors with Sales Agents and Market Realities,” “Why Cinema Still Matters: Activism, Social Relevance and Audience Renewal” and “Gender Equality and the Cost of Inclusion: Who Can Afford to Build a Career in This Industry?” “For many people, algorithms have become synonymous with the death of art. At the same time, there’s another perspective. Used intelligently, data can become a valuable tool rather than a creative constraint,” noted Paolillo. The same is true of AI. “Whether we like it or not, it’s already impacting every stage of the filmmaking process, from development and financing to marketing and distribution. Ignoring it is no longer an option. StepIn wants to create a space where these questions can be discussed openly and honestly, acknowledging both the opportunities and the risks.” The out-of-the-box introduction called “Fear, Lies, and the Illusion of Control” will be delivered by analyst Stephen Follows. “For a century, this industry has bought tools that promise to control the inherent uncertainty in an arts-based business. This has included the use of stars, test screenings, tracking surveys, franchises, and now algorithms,” he told Variety . “My thesis is that while most of them do work to some degree, (a) they don’t work nearly well enough; and (b) the industry uses them wrong. They test what they test and they produce real numbers. Sometimes those numbers even make things marginally better – or at the very least more defensible. The trouble starts with what we do next, because we mistake a marginal edge for control.” He added: “Once you’ve bought a hammer, everything starts to look like a nail, and the questions the tools can answer begin to crowd out the questions that matter. I’m not saying the tools are bullshit – just that we use them wrong. They are expensive comfort, and the side effects often cost more than the edge is worth.” Familiar IP and sequels “do shift the odds,” he noted, but “safe choices still fail all the time, and we never book those failures as risk.” “We call it franchise fatigue or bad marketing, or star casting. Fame genuinely lifts returns, but the star captures most of that uplift in salary. The insurance mostly ends up in the star’s pocket, while the film underneath has become more expensive to save.” Then there’s “the complete misuse and misunderstanding” of the frequently repeated line “nobody knows anything.” “People quote Goldman as if it’s humility and use it as cover for not doing the work,” said Follows. “Right now, there’s a booming trade in certainty. Every stage, every panel, every feed has someone selling the film industry a dream – that this tool, this model, this dataset will finally crack the code. And we are the perfect customers. A hundred years of terrible odds makes people desperate, and desperate people buy dreams.” While the platforms “measure everything and share nothing” – “Netflix has redefined what a ‘view’ is four times and Apple has never published a single audience figure” – people ignore the algorithms that already decide what gets seen. “On the big streaming services, under 6% of titles take around three-quarters of all viewing. The threat is not currently to creation but to discovery. And the one move the machine cannot make is a person with taste saying: ‘This one.’ That’s what festivals are. The counter-algorithm is a human being who gives a damn, and Locarno is full of them.” The opening panel will feature distributor Andrea Occhipinti (Lucky Red), mk2’s Head of Production Yasmine Talli and Doris Ruth Eikhof, professor of cultural economy & policy at the University of Glasgow. “What [Occhipinti] has built with Lucky Red over the past three decades speaks for itself, and the recent partnership between Lucky Red and Studiocanal makes his perspective on consolidation, independent cinema and the changing marketplace particularly timely,” noted Paolillo. Yasmine Talli “has first-hand insight into how ambitious auteur cinema can continue to thrive in an increasingly challenging market,” while Doris Ruth Eikhof is “one of Europe’s leading experts on diversity and inclusion in the cultural economy.” “Statistics about women in film remain discouraging: women are still less likely than men to hold influential positions and be celebrated for their work,” Eikhof told Variety . “It’s important to keep looking at them, as they tell an important story and are powerful evidence, but just focusing on statistics creates an incentive to ‘just bring more women in.’ That’s a big mistake. We need to make sure that women can stay and succeed.” Too often, people tend to take a “one size fits all” approach that dismantles some barriers to women’s opportunity and inclusion but leaves other barriers in place. “We need to support production companies and small businesses to create the conditions in which women of different ages, religions, races and class backgrounds, disabled women, LGBTQ+ women or women with and without caring responsibilities can all do their best work. That’s not a job for statistics. That’s a job we need to do every day, in our workplaces,” said Eikhof. The good news? “It’s possible, we can do it one step at a time, not all of it costs money and it will benefit everybody, not ‘just’ women.” Activism and political engagement will also be discussed, as “the world around us is once again creating a sense of urgency, and filmmakers are responding to it.” “Many of the films that have generated the strongest public debate in recent years have done so not only because of their artistic qualities, but because of the social, political and ethical questions they raise,” noted Paolillo, mentioning the likes of “Parasite,” “The Zone of Interest,” “One Battle After Another,” “Sinners” or “The Voice of Hind Rajab.” “Interestingly, this has also revived an older debate: during this year’s Berlinale, remarks by Wim Wenders, followed in Cannes by comments by Paul Laverty and Park Chan-wook, brought back a question central to the cinema culture of the 1970s: whether films are, by their very nature, political.” Wenders’ comments that filmmakers should “stay out of politics” were widely disputed. “This is something we want to discuss within the broader question whether films are culturally and social relevant in an era shaped by social media, algorithm-driven platforms, fragmented audiences, and an overwhelming flow of images. Does cinema still matter as a cultural and social force? And what strategies can help expand and renew its audience, by finding new ways to engage people across generations?” Overall, Paolillo remains optimistic about the future of film. “I’ve been in this industry long enough to have heard people announce the death of independent cinema countless times. They’re always wrong. Every few years, a new generation of filmmakers, a new movement or a number of unexpected films remind us why cinema still matters,” he argued. That being said, we are now living through a period of “profound transformation.” “The economic model is changing, technology is evolving at an unprecedented pace, and power within the industry is becoming more and more concentrated. We shouldn’t ignore these challenges, but neither should we fear them.” Paolillo added: “That’s ultimately what StepIn is about: bringing together people with very different perspectives, asking difficult questions, challenging assumptions, and collectively imagining what the next chapter of independent cinema could look like.” “I’m genuinely curious to see where this year’s conversations will lead us.” Anonymous Content’s Darren Walker on Company’s 10 Emmy Nominations and Nominee Sally Field’s ‘Motherly’ Dating Advice ‘Today’ Issues ‘Stricter Security Protocols’ for Guests Following Intruder Incident With Craig Melvin (EXCLUSIVE) Mariska Hargitay on Being Courtside for Knicks Game 4 Win: ‘Honored’ and ‘Grateful’ to Say ‘I Was There’ ‘Elle’ Director Jason Moore on Reese Witherspoon’s Set Visit, Season 2’s Archival-Only Wardrobe and What ‘Hardcore’ Fans Can Expect From ‘Murder, She Wrote’ Movie Tom Hanks Says Taylor Swift’s ‘Toy Story 5’ Song Was Kept ‘Top Secret’ From the Cast Until Release Day ‘Kennedy’ Stars Nick Robinson and Laura Donnelly on Why Series Isn’t Leaning Into Family’s Signature Boston Accent Loading comments... Discovery should be blocked in the UK. In The Guardian article , headlined ‘A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that,’ the actors called on Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy to intervene in the $111 billion merger for the good of the British screen industry. It follows Nandy telling UK Parliament that she is “minded to intervene” in the takeover, but she is yet to make a final decision on whether to submit the union to a full public interest investigation. We must not push the public’s interest aside; we must stand up for it and block this merger.” Paramount declined to comment, but a spokesperson pointed to a February open letter CEO David Ellison wrote to the UK creative community, committing to content investment, theatrical windows, and preserving HBO. The actors voiced concerns about the Paramount-Warner merger putting the “livelihoods of thousands of workers” at risk in the UK. They are also anxious about the concentration of news services, given that the combined company would control 5 News, CNN International, and CBS News. “One owner controlling this much of the news, and the truth, endangers the public in a way no ordinary consolidation does,” they said. “And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. title: Benedict Cumberbatch, Alan Cumming, Benedict Wong Pen Op-Ed Urging U.K. to Block “Dangerous” Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All July 27, 2026 1:20am Cumberbatch, Cumming, Wong have called the merger "dangerous." Courtesy of Getty Actors Benedict Cumberbatch , Alan Cumming and Benedict Wong have penned an op-ed in The Guardian calling for the U.K. to block the Paramount – Warner Bros . merger, arguing that the deal threatens to inflict “immense harm on the British public.” The U.K. culture secretary Lisa Nandy — who has remained in her post amid a cabinet reshuffle with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham taking office — has previously said she was “minded to intervene” in the $111 billion mega-deal that, if successful, will undoubtedly change not just Hollywood, but the global film and TV industry. Related Stories Movies Don't Miss the Swiss at Locarno: From a Hunt for Loot, 'The Chilean' and Don Quixote to 'Small Talk' Movies Ontario Wildfires Prompt Mask-Up Orders and Drone Bans on Film Sets -- But Production Rolls On Among a host of issues, the actors cite concerns over the livelihoods of British film and TV crews, independent film financing, and the consolidation of news publications. “As actors and public figures who have spent our careers in the arts in Britain — working with British crews, on British stages and sets — we have a responsibility to the public who support, enjoy and consume the art we make,” wrote the famed Marvel actors (Cumberbatch and Wong), as well as Cummng ( The Traitors ), on Monday in a piece titled “A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that.” “The U.K. is being threatened by a media merger that would harm our workers, our culture and the public — but we can stop it.” They mention that they are encouraged by Nandy’s statements that she wants to investigate the threat to public interest, and acknowledge that she is not acting alone. This month, 12 U.S. states, led by California, sued in federal court to block the merger, warning that it would “raise prices, shrink the number of films made and degrade the quality of what audiences see,” said the men. And over the weekend, news broke that Larry Ellison’s Paramount agreed not to close the takeover until the court decides whether the deal violates antitrust laws. “Their lawsuit confirms the danger; it cannot, however, do the U.K.’s work for it,” continue Cumberbatch, Cumming and Wong, who add that the EU has conditionally backed the merger and makes its own decisions. “The fight against this merger now runs on two fronts, and Nandy commands one of them. Should her department decide to intervene, it may prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for U.K. film, television and media in a generation,” they explain. “This is why. We have spent our lives working in this industry. We know what it looks like from the inside: the sound stages at Leavesden [studio], the crews who move from production to production, the editors and camera operators and costume designers whose names scroll past in the credits at the end of a film. These are our cherished friends and colleagues, who create the shows we all love, who produce the news that educates the public and film the sport events we enjoy together,” write the actors. The men say that U.K. film and TV are not just “images on your screens; they are lives and livelihoods of thousands of workers and families, whose work supports local economies.” They cite buoying figures, such as the 180,000 jobs supported through the industry and the £6.8 billion production spend reported last year. “It is one of the things the U.K. still does better than almost anyone, and a cultural heritage we must protect,” they say. They add that they have watched “with growing alarm” what consolidation does to the “breadth and depth of the work we produce,” before recognizing that independent film acquisitions at the leading independent film festival, Sundance, fell by half between 2019 and 2025. “Award-winning documentaries – films that won Oscars and topped festival juries – have struggled to find commercial distribution because they touched subjects the remaining handful of buyers found inconvenient. Every merger of this kind narrows the funnel through which stories can reach audiences.” To service Warner Bros.’ estimated $84 billion in debt, executives have promised investors around $6bn in “synergies,” Cumberbatch, Cumming and Wong mention. “In plain English, that means redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken,” they add. “That is precisely what makes the Paramount-WBD merger so dangerous,” they write, adding that it has happened so many times before, such as Discovery’s merging with WarnerMedia in 2022, which led to the shelving of finished films and thousands of job losses, or Skydance’s merger with Paramount last year when around 2,000 people were laid off. They admit they are extremely concerned about the consolidation of news outlets like Channel 5, one of the U.K.’s public broadcasters, as well as CNN International . “The CNN and CBS news archives [are] among the world’s most important broadcast news collections, with more than 4.25m videos, images and media spanning nearly half a century of history. If one commercially interested owner controls access to both, they control the raw material of our historical memory… Fold those newsrooms into a single company, and one boardroom’s commercial anxieties — or political debts — determine what millions of people see and what they never learn existed.” “And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. Paramount’s chief executive reportedly told Donald Trump that he would make ‘sweeping changes’ to CNN if the deal went through,” they add. “Actors are often told to stay out of legal arguments,” write Cumberbatch, Cumming and Wong. “We understand the instinct. But we have spent our lives on enough U.K. sets, worked alongside enough U.K. crews and watched enough brilliant work from the U.K. struggle to find a buyer to know that this is not someone else’s argument. It is ours.” THR

title: Don’t Miss the Swiss at Locarno: From a Hunt for Loot, ‘The Chilean’ and Don Quixote to ‘Small Talk’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All July 26, 2026 11:59pm ‘The Chilean’ Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Ready for a bit of Swiss bliss on the big screen? The 79th edition of Switzerland’s Locarno Film Festival is set to be a showcase of adventurous new cinema from around the globe, including homegrown productions from Swiss filmmakers and/or producers. Various sections of the fest, running Aug. 5-16, will serve up homemade cinematic fare. In addition, the popular “Panorama Suisse” section will put the spotlight on “Swiss films that have enjoyed success at festivals, found an audience in cinemas, or are currently released in the country.” Plus, the Locarno Kids Screenings program also includes two titles with Swiss participation. Related Stories Movies Ontario Wildfires Prompt Mask-Up Orders and Drone Bans on Film Sets -- But Production Rolls On TV After Atsuko Okatsuka Came to America, Social Media Knocked Down Barriers to Global Reach For those looking for some Swiss cinematic bliss and trying to avoid having Swiss cheese-sized holes in their Locarno schedules, THR is below highlighting a selection of Swiss treats screening at Locarno79. The Chilean Director: Sergio Castro-San Martín Piazza Grande program International sales: Fandango A political thriller telling the story of a fugitive is ready to explode onto Locarno’s screens. The big-screen epic The Chilean is a co-production between Italy, Chile and Switzerland that starts off in 1976 Chile. Amid mining protests, Aldo, skilled in explosives, is forced into exile, leaving his wife and newborn child behind. He moves to Italy, where he must survive on menial jobs in Torino and where people simply call him Il Cileno, The Chilean. But everything changes when he meets Luciana, a doctor involved with anarchist groups. She offers him the chance to reunite with his family. But in exchange, he must return to his old trade – making bombs for revolutionary groups. “Reconstructing an era means not only designing its atmosphere, but understanding the personalities that embody it,” the director says about The Chilean . “The exiled Aldo Marín leads us to one of the most pressing issues: immigration, omnipresent in the film.” Happiness Is So Close! Director: François-Christophe Marzal Out of competition program International sales: Point Productions ’Happiness Is So Close!,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Jean-Luc, an actor in his 80s, is set to play Don Quixote in a prestigious theater. It is the big role that he has been waiting for to bid farewell to the stage. But his health problems make rehearsals difficult, so the production team hires an understudy in case he is unable to perform. The result is paranoia. Says a synopsis: “Jean-Luc gradually sinks into an obsessive delusion, convinced that his understudy will take his place until he disappears completely.” Jean-Luc Bideau, Gilles Privat and Aurore Clément star in the Swiss production, written by the director and Nicolas Frey, who also served as the editor. Ahead of the Aug. 9 world premiere of Happiness Is So Close! , Bideau will receive a special honorary Leopard at Locarno. Small Talk Director: Matteo Yberra Filmmakers of the Presence Competition program International sales: Urban Sales ‘Small Talk,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival How’s this tease for the hybrid feature that serves up a peek behind the curtain of an elite institution? “Hoping to launch a career in the luxury world, Charlie enrolls at Institut Villa Pierrefeu – the last finishing school still operating in Switzerland. Here, women from all over the world are prepared to move within the circles of the international elite.” Over the course of a summer, their daily life is all about lessons in elegance, protocol and the art of conversation. Written by the director, the actress, along with Louis Rebetez, Hélène Bares, Milan Alfonsi,, the film features actress Hélène Bares. Says the director: “By working with an actress within a real educational setting, the film explores the porous boundary between performance and social behavior, questioning how identity is shaped by learned codes and expectations.” O Jacaré Director: Basil Da Cunha International competition program International sales: Thera Production ‘O Jacaré,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Director Basil Da Cunha has dual Swiss and Portuguese citizenship, which explains this co-production and its elements that don’t sound quintessential Swiss: such as alligators and its setting, namely Reboleira, a suburb of Lisbon. The haul from a robbery has mysteriously disappeared. Within the area sealed off by the police, rumors spread and speculation runs wild. Among the residents, a whole cast of colorful characters dream of getting their hands on the loot. But who will be first to find it? For the filmmaker, who also wrote the script for the movie, the production marks a farewell of sorts. “For the past 15 years, I have been filming the Reboleira neighborhood, which is due to be demolished,” he explains. “ O Jacaré is like a final dance before its disappearance: a vibrant, light-hearted film, infused with comedy and a sense of freedom.” The Angel Maker Director: Marina Klauser Out of competition program International sales: tellfilm ‘The Angel Maker,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival This four-part documentary series from Switzerland, written and directed by Klauser, is not for the faint of heart, but it will appeal to fans of true-crime and cult stories and audiences beyond that. After all, the series tells the story of “the Swiss religious community of Methernitha, which still exists today, its founder Paul Baumann — the inventor of a mysterious energy machine — and the young women who brought him down on charges of child abuse,” as a synopsis reads. Klauser has previously written and directed short films and served as head writer of the writers’ room for the dramedy series How to Be Sad – The Right Way . Frank & Louis Director: Petra Volpe Piazza Grande program International sales: TrustNordisk Kingsley Ben-Adir (left) and Rob Morgan in ‘Frank and Louis.’ Rob Baker Ashton/Courtesy Sundance Last but not least, Locarno will showcase a well-established Swiss cinematic voice’s latest movie, but not in a world premiere, which happened at Sundance. But the film will still get a big square screening at the festival. Swiss-Italian writer-director Petra Volpe followed up her box office and critical success Late Shift with Frank & Louis , her English-language debut, putting a spotlight on another often-overlooked care issue: the care needs of the aging incarcerated. Set within the walls of a U.S. prison, it Frank, portrayed by Kingsley Ben-Adir , who is serving a life sentence and takes on a caretaking role for aging inmates suffering from memory loss. Rob Morgan stars as one of those inmates, Louis. “The theme of care and caretaking, what that means and how we all need it, is such an important societal issue,” Volpe told THR about her motivation for the film in a previous interview. “We take for granted that there are people who take care of us. It’s also a taboo, because nobody wants to think about being old and sick and needy. And especially in the context of prison, we never really think about it deeply.” THR

title: Netflix India Boss Monika Shergill Eyes Global Format Adaptations After “Captive Reality” Series ‘Lock Upp’ Hits 50 Million Hours
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Netflix India Boss Monika Shergill Eyes Global Format Adaptations After “Captive Reality” Series ‘Lock Upp’ Hits 50 Million Hours Carlton Cuse On How Sports Rights Fights Are Hurting Scripted, Fair Residuals, AI & Netflix Series ‘The Secret Of Secrets’ International Insider: Venice Lineup Analysis; Rebel Wilson Legal Victory; Lisa Nandy, Troublemaker-In-Chief View All July 26, 2026 11:30pm Monika Shergill (left) and 'Lock Upp' Netflix EXCLUSIVE: Is Netflix eyeing an Indian version of Love is Blind or Too Hot to Handle ? In an exclusive interview with Deadline, Netflix India VP of Content Monika Shergill revealed her service was working on developing Netflix-owned unscripted formats locally, without revealing their identities. “We are working on a couple of very interesting, big global formats, which are Netflix formats, and they will be coming to India,” she said. While Netflix does not own either Too Hot to Handle and Love is Blind , it the has exclusive international production deals in place for both and has created numerous versions. The underlying format rights remain with Too Hot to Handle program maker Fremantle and The North Road Company-owned Kinetic Content, the maker of Love is Blind . Related Stories News Kalshi Threatens Netflix With Defamation Suit Over "Misleading" Prediction Market Doc Trailer News How 'Ransom Canyon' Season 2's Thomas Rhett & Jordan Davis Music Festival Concert Came Together, Starting With Josh Duhamel Pushed on the identity of the shows, Shergill said: “I am not at liberty to share right now, but something exciting will be announced very soon.” Watch on Deadline The news came as Shergill was outlining the breakout success of another format for which Netflix is rights owner – the Balaji Telefilms -produced “captive reality” show Lock Upp . The show, which debuted on June 27 and will continue playing until August 5, follows celebrity contestants, known as inmates, who live in a jail-themed setting and compete in tasks while facing eliminations. Shergill and Lock Upp creator Ekta Kapoor said the show has become “the most defining entertainment conversation,” with the Netflix chief revealing it has amassed 50 million hours viewed since launch last month (“the equivalent of 5,700 years,” according to Shergill) and accrued 2.5 billion social media interactions within three weeks of launch. The spent two weeks in the Global Top (Non-English) Series list, as Indian unscripted series grow in global popularity. It began with five episodes in the first week, but the “on-audience demand and overwhelming success” has seen this upped to six. “Up to the finale, we’ll just be going nonstop,” she added. Netflix’s most recent What We Watched data dump revealed the show is the second-most watched series by hours. Kapoor, a veteran film and TV producer in India, outlined her theory behind the show’s popularity. “It’s the fact that celebrities are coming in with tags and judgment, and they’re able to discuss that why they are like that, or what has made them like that, so their secrets become their lifelines,” she said. “It’s one way they touch base with their own humanity, their own understanding, their own traumas.” The series actually began life in 2022 on ALTBalaji, the now defunct streamer that Balaji Telefilms operated, and MX Player, which was recently subsumed into Prime Video India. Netflix revitalized it with Bollywood stars Farah Khan and Riteish Deshmukh hosting, and a contestant cast including actors Dheeraj Dhoopar, Shivangi Joshi, Harshad Chopda and Shilpa Shinde. Kapoor was quick to credit Shergill and Netflix for supporting her vision to revive the show, revealing she rejected two other offers to move ahead with the Los Gatos-based streamer. “When you work with a platform, you want to work with a platform that takes your concept or your idea bigger than you thought, and supports your vision,” she said. “For a creator, there is nothing bigger than support – and it doesn’t have to be only financial. It is also because sense of ownership is mutual, and respect is mutual. If make a show for Netflix, I know that Netflix won’t abandon me midway, because it’s not doing well. They will run with me until the last mile.” Pressed by Deadline, Shergill and Kapoor declined to confirm a second season of Lock Upp on Netflix or if the show will be adapted outside of India. However, Shergill did say: “The format is getting a lot of interest internally. I cannot confirm either of those questions, but since it’s doing so well, I think it has a long life.” Comedy focus Besides adapting global formats, Shergill’s other focus at Netflix India is in comedy and growing local talent. One example is stand-up Samay Raina, who first appeared on the streamer on long-running talk series The Great Indian Kapil Show . His chemistry with host and fellow comedian Kapil Sharma was such that Shergill, who had already ordered a stand-up special from him, began a conversation about bringing his YouTube show, India’s Got Latent , to Netflix. A co-exclusive deal for Season 2 was struck, which Shergill calls a “great experiment” and potentially the precusor to similar agreements with both platforms, Raina and his audience all responding positively. “The thinking was very simple, actually,” she said “We really want to be the best home for comedy and the best comedic talent in the country. Samay had come for The Great Indian Kapil Show , and their partnership and that episode worked so well that when we were talking about his stand-up special, and it came up that Latent Season 2 was coming out, it was just intuitive that, uh, the show could exist on Netflix in an ad-free version for his fans. “It just shows that the best kind of creative actually should sit in experiences and different kinds of experiences. We have a huge audience for it on Netflix India.” The Great Indian Kapil Show , which followed on from Sharma’s network shows The Kapil Sharma Show and Comedy Nights with Kapil , is headed for a fifth season and stand-up specials from many of India’s top performers such as Zakir Khan have become top-performing productions. As such, the comedy space “is something that we want to own in India,” said Shergill, and projects are underway wth several big names. While Shergill feels the momentum is with Netflix right now, the service is competing in one of the toughest streaming markets in the world, where JioHotstar, Sony LIV and Prime Video, now including MX Player, are all key players. Indeed, in March 2024, Mike Hopkins, the Head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said India was responsible for new streaming subscribers than anywhere else bar the U.S. for his service. However, only about a quarter of the 601 million streaming consumers in India pay for services, according to Ormax Media research from September 2025, so Netflix has a fight on its hands, but Shergill and her team are taking a bullish outlook. “We’ve been having great momentum,” said. Shergill. “We are one of the most loved entertainment, streaming entertainment services in India. Yes, there is fierce competition, but everyone’s offering and value proposition is different. “What defines Netflix is the ability to do premium and aspirational content and yet make it the most accessible. If I were to just give you a sense of where we are today, the biggest theatrical movies are on Netflix across languages. The biggest premium dramas are on Netflix. The biggest unscripted entertainment is on Netflix today with Kapil Sharma , Lock Upp , Fabulous Lives of Desi Wives and Desi Bling , and the biggest original documentaries consistently are on Netflix. So are most of the awards. “I have great regard for all our competitive services, and we learn a lot from them, but I think the the value and the edge that Netflix brings is our constant experimentation and innovation. No one programs as diversely as we do. No one takes as many bets as we do, whether big, medium or small, and that is what has consistently made our offering the strongest. “We are actually seeing India being one of the biggest growth markets for Netflix all over the world.” ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ While much of the recent focus has been on unscripted, the next big bet from Netflix in India is Operation Safed Sagar , a high-budget military drama series focused on the Indian Air Force’s 1999 aerial campaign during the Kargil War against Pakistan. Shergill calls the show, which is latest in India’s long line of productions on its military prowess, “a very large format VFX extravaganza.” Matchbox Shots and Feel Good Films are making the show in direct collaboration with the Indian Air Force. “The Lock Upp finale is going to be a very big conversation wave in India given the way the pre-finale weeks are looking, and immediately after that, we have Operation Safed Sagar , our biggest show in the tenth year of Netflix in India. There are a whole slew of shows after that, which will be addressing the different audience tastes and moods that we cater to – really the whole spectrum of audience.” Netflix’s Monika Shergill On ‘Lock Upp’ As Indian Series Hits 50M Hours Marvel: Gosling As Ghost Rider; Jonsson In ‘Black Panther 3’; Latest Pics ‘The Odyssey’s $87M+ 2nd Frame Sets Nolan Record, Tops ‘Dark Knight’ Agrees Not To Close WBD Merger Until Next Year; Opponents Cheer Delay Read More About: Comments

title: ‘President Curtis’ Creator Dan Harmon on Trump, Obama Influencing Show and His Vision for ‘Rick and Morty’ Movie
full_text: Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All July 26, 2026 10:21pm A scene from Adult Swim's 'Rick and Morty' spinoff 'President Curtis.' Courtesy of Adult Swim Logo text President Curtis is getting sworn into the Rick and Morty universe. Veteran actor Keith David voices the titular commander in chief on President Curtis , the Rick and Morty spinoff that premiered Sunday on Adult Swim following the season nine finale for the flagship series. Stephanie Beatriz and Jim Rash round out the cast for the new project that centers on the leader of the free world and his quirky staff as they navigate an array of unusual crises. David originated the role of President Andre Curtis during a season two episode of Rick and Morty back in 2015 and has continued to return periodically throughout the series. President Curtis co-creator James Siciliano recalls talk of a spinoff happening as a natural extension of the Rick and Morty team working on the Thanksgiving episode for season five, with Rick seeking a presidential turkey pardon. Related Stories Movies The Doom Boom: Marvel Studios Brings 'Doomsday' and More to Its Most Crowded Comic-Con Panel Ever Movies Ryan Reynolds' Deadpool Crashes Comic-Con to Beg for 'Avengers: Doomsday' Role “We started to see a more dialed-in world for Curtis there, with spider-FDR, the French assassin hidden in the Statue of Liberty — the National Treasure element of that stuff,” Siciliano, a longtime member of the Rick and Morty staff, tells The Hollywood Reporter . “We could see more of an X Files world that could be built out and wouldn’t necessarily be redundant with the Rick and Morty universe.” President Curtis Courtesy of Adult Swim Siciliano and fellow President Curtis series creator Dan Harmon recall the writing team initially suggesting qualities that have cemented previous real-life U.S. presidents as particularly memorable. Harmon notes that he personally has been fascinated by Harry S. Truman, while other writers brought up Teddy Roosevelt — and, of course, Donald Trump and Barack Obama . “The conversations about Obama and Trump were inevitable,” Harmon admits. “Curtis has a naïveté that you could overlap with Trump, who is like, ‘I’m an outsider, and I consider this job simple, and I don’t care about the bureaucracy of it.’ On the Obama side, it’s the charmer and the guy who gets organic joy in being liked — that whole rock star aspect of Obama. But mostly just more legendary aspects of presidents from the past, all Serpentor’d into a test tube baby that then becomes our version of maybe Martin Sheen in West Wing , where it’s our fantasy president, warts and all.” For fans hoping to catch Rick and Morty popping up on President Curtis (mild spoilers ahead), rest assured that the adventure-seeking duo are indeed part of the pilot, although they will not appear again in the first season. Luckily, there is more President Curtis to come, as the show’s team announced Saturday at San Diego Comic-Con that the spinoff had scored an early renewal for a second season . Rick and Morty Everett “If we didn’t do that, people would be waiting for it,” Siciliano says of writing Rick and Morty into the President Curtis pilot. “In the first season, that’s their only appearance, but that’s not to say that we have anything against them appearing in the future. We really wanted to have this show just be able to get its own identity and breathe a little bit, so that people felt like it was its own show.” Harmon concurs: “If the show has a life of its own, then we can go Dick Wolf nuts with the crossovers and have Detective Munch all over SVU . But we look forward to earning that.” The President Curtis launch arrives just weeks after Rick and Morty landed its third Emmy Award nomination for best animated series, having won in 2018 and 2020. This year marks the show’s first such nomination after a turbulent stretch in recent years that saw Justin Roiland (who co-created the series with Harmon) exit following felony domestic abuse charges that have since been dismissed. The titular voice roles were recast in light of Roiland’s firing, with Ian Cardoni replacing him as inventor Rick Sanchez, while Harry Belden took over as teen grandson Morty. “It is an incredibly important nomination for us because the show has gone through transitions of such peril,” Harmon candidly shares. “To me, it feels like we are an athlete back on a field after a major injury, and so it is an honor to be nominated. It is all I need. I’m happy to go and watch Smiling Friends win or whatever the case, but I’m so grateful for that nomination.” President Curtis Courtesy of Adult Swim President Curtis is not the only potential opportunity for expansion for the Rick and Morty world. THR recently reported that supervising director Jacob Hair was in talks to helm an animated feature version of the series for Warner Bros. Although the possible film does not yet have a script, Harmon notes that it does have “a technically approved idea that we’re dreaming away on.” He was late to checking out Denis Villeneuve’s Dune films but reveals that they now might serve as inspiration: “I just watched the Dune movies because of messing around with the Rick and Morty movie script. I was like, ‘Oh, my God, I’m so late to Dune.’ It’s so rad.” As for his hopes with the Rick and Morty film, Harmon adds, “It would be my goal, however self-destructive, to make it the greatest movie ever to exist. That might make it hard to write. It would probably be a sci-fi epic, transcending time and space, but not in a way that was unsatisfying. It would probably blend colors as varied in its palette as Lethal Weapon 2 and Dune 2: Toon , as well as Indiana Jones and everything. One could argue that it’s a concept that would be my undoing and the franchise’s as well, since me having permission to think about stuff is not the recipe for success that people would think. It’s more of a trailhead to hell, traditionally.” THR

title: Dylan Mulvaney Responds After Trump Mocks Her and CNN’s Kaitlan Collins at White House Correspondents’ Dinner
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All July 26, 2026 8:59pm Dylan Mulvaney Maya Dehlin Spach/Getty Images Transgender advocate and actress Dylan Mulvaney has responded to President Donald Trump after the latter mocked both her and CNN’s Kaitlan Collins during his speech at the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner on Friday night. At the event, which had been postponed from April after a gunman fired shots as the first dinner was under way, Trump gave a speech wherein he compared the two women after Collins accepted an award for her working covering the administration.. “I want to personally congratulate CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on receiving her award,” Trump said. “It was all about me. It’s a fake — she shouldn’t get the award, it was a fake. But I didn’t mind. I said, ‘Kaitlan, congratulations.’ But it was fake, there’s no question about it.” Related Stories News President Trump Roasts Media at Rescheduled, Pared-Down White House Correspondents' Dinner News Spencer Pratt Tears Into Gavin Newsom, Rob Bonta Over Paramount Lawsuit in Lengthy Video Rant After criticizing Collins for her facial expressions, Trump then compared her to Mulvaney, mentioning the 2023 controversy surrounding the latter’s Bud Light commercial . Three years ago, Mulvaney made an ad for Bud Light that was met with criticism from conservatives who launched a boycott against the beer brand, leading to a decline in sales. “I thought Kaitlan had really made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn’t her on the Bud Light can, it was Dylan Mulvaney,” Trump said Friday. “Dylan Mulvaney cost Bud Light $35 billion in market cap. That was the worst commercial ever made by the way, for those few people who want to hear that. Most people don’t care, but I would. I wouldn’t want to hire Dylan any time soon.” For her part, Collins posted a series of photos on Instagram after the event that included a quote from Eleanor Roosevelt: “No one can make you feel inferior without your consent.” She captioned the post: “he second best part of last night’s White House Correspondents Dinner was receiving an award from my friend and mentor, @wolfblitzer. The first was reminding everyone why the First Amendment — and asking uncomfortable questions that people in power don’t like — matters.” On Sunday morning, Trump doubled down on his comparison of the two women, posting a photo of Mulvaney from her Bud Light ad that had been edited to show Collins’ face on Mulvaney’s body. Later that day, Mulvaney posted a nearly four-minute video on social media in which she noted that Trump had mentioned her four times on Friday night and she felt the need to respond. She started by congratulating Collins on her award and giving her praise. “I would like to … tell her that I’m incredibly honored to be compared to her in any way, and I hope that she keeps doing all the great work,” Mulvaney said. Mulvaney continued: “Now, the president also brought up a video I did over three years ago, and mind you, I’ve been kind of flying under the radar, keeping up a pretty low profile, just like doing my little musicals, singing, dancing. And yet I am still his topic of conversation all these years later. And it seems to me that I might be like the one that got away for these men. Like, I am permanently burned into their retinas. I am microchipped into their minds.” Mulvaney noted that a few weeks ago, she might have been more upset about Trump’s comments, but shared that she’d been “ghosted last month by a hookup who I really liked,” which taught her something about how she wanted to be treated. “What I realized from that experience was that I shouldn’t want to be with someone who doesn’t really want to be with me,” she said. “So maybe I shouldn’t want to be professionally supported by an administration that doesn’t personally support me or so many others in this country. Food for thought. In fact, maybe being publicly mocked and criticized by this administration is actually like the greatest compliment of all, because it puts me in the company of some of like the most brilliant, empathetic people in our world today.” She continued: “But I do still wonder, like, why is it so important to them that I don’t find success? Like, what is it that I have that they don’t? Oh my God, freedom. I am free in a way that they will never have the privilege to experience, and they want to use their power to take away my freedom, but what they don’t understand is that my freedom has like zero contingency on what they can provide for me because my freedom is fully dependent on the moment that I acknowledged my real authentic self and every day since. And sharing that with the world, it’s just icing on the cake, but they don’t want me to be able to share that because it would mean young people realizing that if someone like me can be themselves and find success and freedom, then they can find success and freedom for themselves too.” She wrapped up her video by encouraging viewers to support trans and non-binary people. “And lastly, to the president, thank you for reminding me that I am more powerful than I even knew,” she added. Watch her video below. @dylanmulvaney A response 🇺🇸❤️ please support trans and non binary people today and every day ♬ I Am America – Shea Diamond THR

title: ‘Dungeons & Dragons’ Writer-Director Reveals Sequel Has Been Written, Hasn’t Been Made For “Financial Reasons”
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Dungeons & Dragons’ Writer-Director Reveals Sequel Has Been Written, Hasn’t Been Made For “Financial Reasons” Dylan Mulvaney Responds To Trump’s WHCD “Diss Track,” Feels Like “The One That Got Away” For MAGA Men Mary Beth Barone Says She & Benito Skinner Tried To “Get Out” Of ‘Ride’ Podcast Contract Over Dear Media CEO’s Politics: “Hard To Reconcile That” View All July 26, 2026 8:05pm Michelle Rodriguez, Justice Smith, Chris Pine and Sophia Lillis in 'Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves' (2023) Aidan Monaghan/Paramount Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection After three years, Dungeons & Dragons has another campaign in store for fans of the 2023 movie… if it can just get the greenlight. Jonathan Goldstein , who co-wrote and co-directed Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves with John Francis Daley, revealed at Comic-Con that they wrote a sequel to their 2023 adaptation of the tabletop role-playing game. “We actually wrote a sequel to Dungeons & Dragons . We were hired to write it,” Goldstein told ScreenRant . “I don’t know that it will see the light of day for a number of financial reasons. title: Dylan Mulvaney Responds To Trump’s WHCD “Diss Track,” Feels Like “The One That Got Away” For MAGA Men

Mandel Ngan/AFP/Mike Marsland/WireImage More than three years after sparking conservative backlash with her Bud Light social media partnership, Dylan Mulvaney was as surprised as anyone to hear her name in Donald Trump ‘s mouth at the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner. Counting “four times” the POTUS mentioned her name in his speech on Friday, the Broadway actress, TikTok personality and transgender advocate reacted to being “the one that got away” for MAGA men after Trump attempted to roast her in his hour-long “diss track” at the WHCA’s annual event. “Firstly, I would like to congratulate CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on her award and tell her that I’m incredibly honored to be compared to her in any way, and I hope that she keeps doing all the great work,” prefaced Mulvaney in a TikTok video . Related Stories News Donald Trump Delivers Rally-Like Hour Of Rehash In White House Correspondents’ Dinner Speech Politics Dylan Mulvaney Addresses Firestorm Of Hate Sparked By Bud Light Endorsement For The First Time After the WHCA awarded Collins the Excellence in Presidential News Coverage Under Deadline Pressure, Trump joked in his set that he “thought Kaitlan had really made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn’t her on the Bud Light can, it was Dylan Mulvaney,” to which the audience had no reaction. Watch on Deadline “And Dylan Mulaney cost Bud Light $35 billion dollar in market cap,” Trump continued as the crowd stayed silent. “That was the worst commercial ever made, by the way, for those few people that want to hear that. Most people don’t care, but I would. I wouldn’t want to hire Dylan anytime soon. Think of it, they hired Dylan Mulaney and their market cap has gone down by $35 billion. Who wrote that commercial?” @dylanmulvaney A response 🇺🇸❤️ please support trans and non binary people today and every day ♬ I Am America – Shea Diamond Noting the Bud Light video Trump mentioned was more than three years ago, Mulvaney said in her video, “Mind you, I’ve been kind of flying under the radar, keeping up a pretty low profile, just doing my little musicals, singing, dancing, and yet I am still his topic of conversation all these years later. It seems to me that I might be like the one that got away for these men. I am permanently burned into their retinas. I am microchipped into their minds.” Mulvaney added, “Maybe being publicly mocked and criticized by this administration is actually the greatest compliment of all, because it puts me in the company of some of the most brilliant, empathetic people in our world today. … They want to use their power to take away my freedom. But what they don’t understand is that my freedom has zero contingency on what they can provide for me, because my freedom is fully dependent on the moment that I acknowledged my real authentic self and every day since, and sharing that with the world is the icing on the cake. “They don’t want me to be able to share that,” she continued. “Because it would mean young people realizing that, if someone like me can be themselves and find success and freedom, then they can find success and freedom for themselves too.” In April 2023, Bud Light sent a can of their beer with Mulvaney’s face on it to her, which she featured in a TikTok video, prompting intense conservative backlash and a boycott of the brand.
