title: ‘House Of The Dragon’s Benjamin Evan Ainsworth Discusses Daeron Targaryen’s Choices & Future Motives As Season 3 Hits Home Stretch
full_text: Skip to main content By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Major League Soccer Boards Danny Ramirez Soccer Drama ‘Baton’ As Key Partner Artists Equity, Hidden Content, Ultraboom Media And Icki Eneo Arlo Partner On Doc ‘Shot in the Dark’, Following First U.S. Paralympic Blind Soccer Team Sony Pictures Circling Ridley Scott’s ‘Treasure Island’ Package Starring Hugh Jackman View All July 26, 2026 7:01pm Benjamin Evan Ainsworth as Daeron Targaryen in 'House of the Dragon' Courtesy of HBO SPOILER ALERT: This story contains details from episode 6 of House of the Dragon on HBO . With only two episodes left of the third season of HBO’s House of the Dragon, the pieces are falling in to place for Ormund Hightower (James Norton) as Daeron Targaryen ( Benjamin Evan Ainsworth ) watches in the wings. Related Stories News ‘House of the Dragon’ Season 3 Release Schedule: When Do New Episodes Air? Festivals 25 Tons Of Propane, 314 Shooting Days & Lots Of Practical Naval Warfare: How Ryan Condal & Team Pulled Off ‘House Of The Dragon’ Season 3 — ATX TV Festival In the first half of the season, Targaryen kept his guard up and was mindful of his actions in front of his captor, fearing harm may come to him by Hightower if he mades any missteps. On Sunday’s episode, he is finally able to tell someone these fears as his uncle, Ser Gwayne Hightower, vistits Tumbleton to give updates on the war throughout Westeros. Daeron makes it clear to his uncle that he has only been following Ormund’s orders and agreeing with his decisions for self-preservation, not because what Ormund is doing is right. He also lets it be known to Gwayne that while Ormund tells him all this is being done so Daeron can take his seat on the Iron Throne, he is very aware that the chances of becoming king one day are highly unlikely. Watch on Deadline The episode also features a failed assassination attempt on Ormund by Rhaenyra that is thwarted by Gwayne. The scene ends with a number of dead bodies and also shows Gwayne and Daeron how Ormund feels about lost limbs and blood as he vomits in front of them. Ainsworth sat down with Deadline to discuss this week’s episode, including if his character admires some of the schemes Ormund is plotting, his first season on the show, and whether there is more drama to come in Tumbleton before the season comes to an end. DEADLINE: Congrats on the first season Ben, how are you finding it so far? BENJAMIN EVAN AINSWORTH: Well, it’s been it’s been an honor, really. I was a huge fan of Game of Thrones and the first two seasons of Dragon , so I kind of came into the audition process as a fan. So when it came to doing the audition, it was like, the coolest thing ever in itself, but now to be here, having wrapped and watching these episodes come out and seeing the reception, it has been kind of like a whirlwind, but a dream come true. DEADLINE : So the first five episodes, it’s pretty clear Daeron is minding his steps when he’s around Ormond. This is the episode where he’s finally able to say, “I feel like a puppet” and “I’m only doing these things so he doesn’t harm me.”Is he in complete survival mode right now? Or is there a part of him that kind of like weirdly admires the way Ormond is playing the Game of Thrones? AINSWORTH : I think the relationship he has with Ormond is twisted and controlling and manipulative in many ways, but I think it has a bedrock of love that’s binding it together. However warped it may be, I remember in episode 4 where in the beginning he’s kind of talking to the people of Tumbleton and gelding the man who had who had done wrong. There’s almost like a pride and an admiration there in a moment like that. But then the complete opposite, in another moment, where he’s being forced to kill Leo by Ormond. I think he has his guard up all the time with Ormond. He has to, because anything could happen at any moment. He’s had to learn how to deal with him as a character out of survival. There is an aspect of him which has an admiration and wants to be admired by Ormond as well. He’s a 17-year-old kid who’s has no parental figures. He’s sent away from his mother and I think he longs for that kind of affection. DEADLINE: So Ormond’s assassins are raising havoc in King’s Landing, killing Daemon’s men under Ormond’s orders, but in the name of King Daeron. Do you actually think he has the aspirations to be king or, if he had a choice, would he rather just be a high lord and just not have bear the responsibility? AINSWORTH : If you asked him two weeks before Season 3, he would never have dreamed of being king. It wasn’t on his mind. This kind of prospect has been thrust upon him in this season. He’s been thrown in the middle of the dance between Hightower and Targaryen. I think he’s still kind of grappling with the shock of it as well as questioning himself. What do I want? I find kind of that one was more interesting than the answer in many ways, the aspect of him coming of age and figuring out who he is through this chaotic time. But if he were to think about being king, it comes from a position of almost getting out of this domineering relationship. Like a sense of freedom away from that. I suppose leading with his awareness, with his kind of empathy, but also I think he has no idea nor decided on any path. DEADLINE: You’ve spent a lot of this season basically talking a lot; there’s not a lot of action going on. You get your first big set piece even though you’re not quite involved, more of an observer. While it’s an awesome scene, there’s a very important moment, I feel, where we see how Orman reacts when he’s in a situation like this. The actual sight of blood and dead bodies makes him vomit. I’m curious, while Daeron looks rattled because of what he just witnessed, he looks over and part of me wonders, does Daeron now see Orman as a weaker leader, and not this powerful person? Does that moment give Daeron thoughts about how he can control the situation and maybe get out of this because of how Orman reacts in that moment? AINSWORTH : I think it’s definitely a change in the way Daeron is seeing things. A lot of it is the shock of the moment, but also there is certainly something to the idea that I’ve been controlled and kind of molded by this person. As soon things become real and dangerous, he’s debilitated. And so there’s almost a frustration with that. How can I be controlled by someone who has been taken out this easily? I don’t think it computes to something directly I can use against him in that moment, but I suppose it really feels like a kettle boiling in this episode. The power dynamics are really kind of teetering and getting closer to switching the other way. DEADLINE: I wanted to talk about the filming in general. This is your first season and this show is so broad in scope and epic action scenes, dragons, etc. I find it fascinating for you and James, it’s almost like a play where it’s grounded, you’re almost in the same room the whole time talking. Has it helped with this being your first season on the show for the two of you? To be slowly moved in where you’re not involved with these grand battles and stuff where you’re able to kind of find your footing as character,s or are you a little jealous when you see your co-stars flying dragons and in big battles? AINSWORTH : Oh, yeah, good question. I don’t know. To be able to have your group and to be able to move around the world with your couple of actors, it just means that I’ve found at least that I’ve made these great connections between the characters, but also just as people on set, to be able to be together and have scenes where it’s just the four of us for half the show, I think it makes it easy to make communities. DEADLINE: Is there one big move we can expect from Daeron within this home stretch or is it too early to say with what will come with him and Ormond? AINSWORTH : I think the stage is set for a fun finish, certainly in Tumbleton. So, yeah, keep an eye on Gwayne and Daeron’s relationship and whatever Orman’s got cooking in the oven. I hope fans enjoy the last couple episodes. title: On Heels of World Cup, Polo Star Nacho Figueras Says Horseback Sport Has “All the Ingredients to Be the Next Big Thing”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tim Chan Plus Icon Tim Chan @mrtimchan Follow Sign Up View All July 26, 2026 6:57pm Nacho Figueras and Aurora Figueras Blaquier join St. Regis Hotels & Resorts in celebrating the St. Regis British Open for The Cowdrey Gold Cup Polo Final at Cowdray Park Polo Club on July 19, 2026 in Midhurst, England. Dave Benett Polo legend Nacho Figueras says the centuries-old horseback sport could finally be poised for a mainstream breakthrough thanks to the recent success of the World Cup . Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter at The St. Regis British Open Polo Championship for the Cowdray Gold Cup in the UK last weekend, Figueras says the resounding buzz and fan engagement around the World Cup has him believing that polo could find a similar audience. “I think it’s been an incredible moment for sports in America,” he says, also citing the New York Knicks’ recent NBA championship win. “People are learning to love sports events, especially when it’s very well put together, and polo, I think, has all the ingredients to be the next big thing.” Related Stories TV WNBA on Sling TV: Here's How to Watch the 2026 WNBA All-Star Game Live Online TV Spain Scores World Cup Docuseries at Prime Video While Figueras appeared in the 2024 Prince Harry-produced Netflix documentary, Polo , the Argentine sporting icon says he’s working on his own real-life project to “bring polo to the cities.” Describing it as “Formula 1 meets Sail GP meets Padal [and] mixed with the Longines equestrian series ,” the polo star says he envisions events that will be “like the F1 version of polo,” complete with a film crew to capture how it all comes together. “The idea is to do a Drive to Survive -type thing, because I think that giving people access to our kitchen and the kitchens of the athletes, really helps you feel connected to the person on the horse,” he says. Plus, he adds, “Polo has horses, good looking men and women, athleticism and beautiful spots [where the matches take place]. What else could you want?” Assouline ASSOULINE CLASSICS COLLECTION Polo Heritage Co-written by Figueras $120 Buy Now AT ASSOULINE Figueras was among the VIP guests taking in the Cowdray Gold Cup in West Sussex last weekend from the St. Regis tent. As the official “St. Regis Connoisseur ,” the athlete and model got to enjoy a rare day off from the polo field, instead watching the proceedings alongside stars like Andrew Scott, Gwendoline Christie, British designer Giles Deacon and writer Jack Guinness, who all enjoyed storied St. Regis rituals like a champagne sabrage, and sips of the brand’s signature Bloody Mary (the tomato-based cocktail was said to have originated in the U.S. at the King Cole Room inside the St. Regis Hotel in New York in 1934). Giles Deacon, Gwendoline Christie, Jack Guinness and Andrew Scott at the St. Regis British Open for The Cowdrey Gold Cup Polo Final at Cowdray Park Polo Club on July 19, 2026 in Midhurst, England. Photo by Dave Benett Guests at the polo event also got a preview of the St. Regis London, expected to open in the city’s Mayfair neighborhood this fall. Occupying the former Westbury Hotel location at the intersection of Bond Street and Conduit Street, the new property will feature 193 guest rooms inspired by its Savile Row and luxury fashion house and auction house surroundings. The property will also open with Le Perroquet, a French brasserie-style restaurant from acclaimed Chef Daniel Rose, best known for La Bourse et La Vie in Paris and the Michelin-starred Le Coucou in New York. “St. Regis is an old brand with heritage, with family values, and with an actual history and connection to polo,” Figueras says, noting that the hotel chain’s founding family, the Astors, were a prominent fixture at polo matches on New York’s Governors Island. “This event and this partnership just makes sense.” Agata Noweta Studio The Gaston Polo Team, led by Chilean patron Jean Paul Luksic, was crowned Cowdray Gold Cup champions after a nail-biting 9-8 victory over the previously unbeaten Dubai Polo Team. While Figueras was mum on who he was cheering for — explaining that he has friends and fellow Argentine players on both teams — he says the weekend event in England was further proof that the sport is ready for a U.S. invasion. And in addition to his planned polo event series and documentary, Figueras says he has one other idea he’d like to pitch. “I feel very bullish about doing a scripted thing,” the memorable Gossip Girl guest star says, noting that, “what Yellowstone did for Western was incredible. I would love to work with a guy like Taylor Sheridan, who is really one of the most incredible storytellers out there and who loves horses, and say, ‘Hey, I think that polo could be a perfect anchor for one of your amazing shows.” “I also love Succession ,” Figueras adds, “so I believe that this polo show could be the perfect marriage between Yellowstone and Succession .” Has he been in touch with Sheridan? “No, I don’t know him, so maybe this [article] will help,” the dashing polo star says with his magazine-cover smile. “Taylor when you read this, please get in touch.” THR

title: Martin Scorsese Stars in ‘Family Blend’ Directed by Daughter Francesca for Coffee Brand Lavazza
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All July 26, 2026 4:53pm Francesca Scorsese and Martin Scorsese attend the 5th annual Academy Museum Gala at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles on Oct. 18, 2025. (Photo by Amy Sussman/Getty Images) Lights, camera, caffeinate. Martin Scorsese took a break from the director’s chair to step in front of the camera for a change for Lavazza’s new branded miniseries Family Blend celebrating “the magic of coffee.” True to its title, Scorsese isn’t alone in the project as it’s directed by and co-starring his daughter, Francesca Scorsese . A few other famous faces help fill out the five-episode project, including Jason Biggs and Adrien Brody . There’s a lot of blending going on, too, in the locations and content as Francesca filmed the branded series in places that have helped shape her father’s life and creative efforts, like the Little Italy neighborhood in New York and his own virtual production center in Brooklyn. Per Lavazza, the series is meant to explore “the deep bond, shared memories and passing of the torch between two artistic visions” with coffee playing a prominent role. But they also get a playful assist from familial banter. Related Stories Movies Ellen Burstyn to Receive Venice Lifetime Golden Lion Movies "The White Devil" Takes Karlovy Vary: Robert Richardson Receives Honor From a Paper-Ripping Harvey Keitel “The Family Blend series shows how coffee acts as a universal bridge, bringing together different stories and creative visions,” said Lavazza Group chief marketing officer Carlo Colpo of the project, which aligns with the brand’s communication platform “Pleasure Makes Us Human.” “With this project, we are thrilled to portray coffee as a cultural gesture that spans generations and languages, serving as a meeting point for creativity and identity. The collaboration with Martin and Francesca Scorsese brings to life a unique dialogue that blends the depth of cinematic language with modern digital formats.” Credit for Family Blend goes to Romilda De Luca of RDL Worldwide/Publicis Group and Lisa Frechette of Sikelia Productions. Propagate Content produced the series with Ben Silverman, Howard T. Owens and Drew Buckley producing on behalf of that company. Maruri Group helped develop the creative vision with support from Joey Payne. The first episode dropped earlier this week, with new installments rolling out once a month through November on the brand’s and talents’ global social channels. See the first one, “But First … Coffee,” below. It was filmed at Martin Scorsese NYU Virtual Production Center in Brooklyn, New York, a site launched in fall 2024 by NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts. “Elizabeth Street,” which drops in August, features a nostalgic walk down the street where Martin grew up with his parents amid the “relentless chaos of New York constantly interrupting their talk.” “Back to Tisch,” releasing in September, finds the father and daughter returning to their alma mater, NYU, in the 1960s. The October release of “Where Everybody Knows Your Name” finds Francesca offering a tour inside Di Palo’s Fine Foods in Little Italy while waiting on her father. Lastly, in November comes “But Last … Coffee,” a finale set in an iconic New York cafe where Francesca (joined by Biggs) challenges her father to break his strict black coffee routine and try new blends and modern preparations. Francesca previously directed the shorts Crimson Ties and Fish Out of Water and an episode of Martin Scorsese Presents: The Saints. THR

During a recent interview on the Dish Podcast , the actor said he’s been “absolutely loving” his press tours this summer for The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day because he’s really proud of those movies. But he can’t say that about all the projects in his filmography. “When you’re doing press for movies you’re really proud of, it’s really easy,” he explained. “Because when they ask you questions about why should people go and watch this movie, you’re not lying to anyone. Holland didn’t name the specific films he was referring to, as he would have much rather continued the high praise of his latest pics. “It’s felt really like a bit of a victory lap, to be honest,” Holland said of The Odyssey and Brand New Day . “I’ve really enjoyed it. I’m super proud of both of the films.” The Christopher Nolan-directed pic , based on Homer’s ancient Greek poem, follows King Odysseus’ (Matt Damon) dangerous voyage back to Ithaca after the Trojan War, including battles with mythical creatures, as he attempts to reunite with his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), and son, Telemachus ( Holland). The film also stars Zendaya, Robert Pattinson, Charlize Theron, Lupita Nyong’o, John Leguizamo , Elliot Page, Mia Goth, Corey Hawkins, Jon Bernthal , Samantha Morton, Travis Scott and Benny Safdie. Since The Odyssey has already hit theaters — where it’s been dominating, sailing past $600 million globally in its second weekend — The Crowded Room actor has turned his attention back to Spider-Man promotion, which releases on July 31. But he’s still grateful for everything he’s learned from his Odyssey co-stars throughout the film’s respective press tour. “I’ve had the pleasure of sitting down with Anne Hathaway for the last three days and doing press with her,” Holland said. “For me, that’s been an awesome learning experience. She’s such a pro.” As for Brand New Day , Holland reunites with his wife, Zendaya, onscreen and Jacob Batalon for the fourth installment. The film sees Holland’s Peter Parker living entirely alone as Spider-Man in a world that doesn’t remember him. That’s until mounting pressure of seeing his old friends move on without him triggers a dangerous change, while a powerful new villain emerges. THR

full_text: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that The Paramount-Warner Bros merger is being fought in the US and UK. Britain’s culture secretary knows the risks and can intervene. She should View image in fullscreen Though it has yet to become front-page news in the UK, you should know about the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros merger . It threatens to inflict immense harm on the British public. As actors and public figures who have spent our careers in the arts in Britain – working with British crews, on British stages and sets – we have a responsibility to the public who support, enjoy and consume the art we make. The UK is being threatened by a media merger that would harm our workers, our culture and the public – but we can stop it. We are encouraged by Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, who recently sent letters to Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery , as well as a statement to parliament , indicating that she is “minded to intervene” in Paramount’s $110bn takeover of Warner Bros. She is correct to investigate this major threat to the UK’s public interest. And she will not be acting alone. This month, 12 US states, led by California, sued in federal court to block the merger, warning that it would raise prices, shrink the number of films made and degrade the quality of what audiences see. And they just won a major victory: on Friday, Paramount agreed to delay the merger until trial, which could be months. These states acted even after Washington’s own justice department – despite the reported reservations of career staff – waved the deal through . Their lawsuit confirms the danger; it cannot, however, do the UK’s work for it. US courts fight on the antitrust front for US markets. The EU, which last week conditionally backed the merger , also makes its own decisions. The UK’s public interest, our public service broadcasting, our news plurality, the plurality of voices British audiences hear, can only be defended here, by our own secretary of state and the Competition and Markets Authority. The fight against this merger now runs on two fronts, and Nandy commands one of them. Should her department decide to intervene, it may prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for UK film, television and media in a generation. This is why. We have spent our lives working in this industry. We know what it looks like from the inside: the sound stages at Leavesden, the crews who move from production to production, the editors and camera operators and costume designers whose names scroll past in the credits at the end of a film. These are our cherished friends and colleagues, who create the shows we all love, who produce the news that educates the public and film the sport events we enjoy together. UK film and television are not just images on your screens; they are the lives and livelihoods of thousands of workers and families, whose work supports local economies. The industry supports more than 180,000 jobs , generated £6.8bn in production spend last year alone and adds roughly £12bn a year in value to our economy. It is one of the things the UK still does better than almost anyone, and a cultural heritage we must protect. We have watched, with growing alarm, what consolidation does to the breadth and depth of the work we produce: independent film acquisitions at the leading independent film festival Sundance fell by half between 2019 and 2025. Award-winning documentaries – films that won Oscars and topped festival juries – have struggled to find commercial distribution because they touched subjects the remaining handful of buyers found inconvenient. Every merger of this kind narrows the funnel through which stories can reach audiences. That is precisely what makes the Paramount-WBD merger so dangerous. It’s why the intervention of Nandy and her department matters so much. Paramount proposes to swallow Warner Bros Discovery in one of the largest leveraged buyouts ever attempted, loading the combined company with an estimated $84bn in debt . To service it, executives have promised investors around $6bn in “ synergies ”. In plain English, that means redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken. We have seen this before. When Discovery merged with WarnerMedia in 2022, it shelved finished films and cut thousands of jobs ; when Skydance merged with Paramount last year, it laid off about 2,000 people . Now the same executives are making the same promise, and UK crews, producers, talent and audiences will pay when the bill comes due. But jobs are mostly a matter for the Competition and Markets Authority, whose review should end in a full phase 2 investigation. The job of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport goes further: to determine whether the merger is in the public interest. It most certainly is not. In her statement to British MPs , Nandy cited the need for a sufficient plurality of views in news media and a sufficient plurality of individuals controlling media enterprises. She has also highlighted the potential impact on streaming services, content homogenisation and children’s television. The Enterprise Act protects something we should all care about: who decides what we get to watch, and what we get to know. Consider the breadth of what this single company would hold. Channel 5, one of our five public service broadcasters , which serves the evening news to people without the cost of a subscription. CNN International, which Ofcom research in 2018 found UK viewers rated above every other TV news source for quality, accuracy, trustworthiness and impartiality. The CNN and CBS news archives – among the world’s most important broadcast news collections, with more than 4.25m videos, images and media spanning nearly half a century of history. If one commercially interested owner controls access to both, they control the raw material of our historical memory. One owner controlling this much of the news, and the truth, endangers the public in a way no ordinary consolidation does. When separate owners run separate newsrooms, a story judged inconvenient by one can still reach audiences through another. Fold those newsrooms into a single company, and one boardroom’s commercial anxieties – or political debts – determine what millions of people see and what they never learn existed. And we know something about this particular proprietor’s intentions. Paramount’s chief executive reportedly told Donald Trump that he would make “ sweeping changes ” to CNN if the deal went through. When the buyer of the world’s most trusted international news channel makes editorial promises to a politician, a British secretary of state is entitled – and, really, obliged – to ask questions before the ink dries. Nandy has been scrupulous in noting that no final decision has been taken. Good. It is important to take the time to get this right. But the case for a full public interest intervention, with Ofcom assessing plurality and reporting back, is overwhelming. Actors are often told to stay out of legal arguments. We understand the instinct. But we have spent our lives on enough UK sets, worked alongside enough UK crews and watched enough brilliant work from the UK struggle to find a buyer to know that this is not someone else’s argument. It is ours. Nandy has opened the door to intervention. She must walk through it, for the sake of everyone who makes UK television and film – and everyone who watches it. If she does not, we will be left without the ability to protect our industry and our culture from this consolidation. We must not push the public’s interest aside; we must stand up for it and block this merger.
